standard.title: Interaction skills for challenging meaning
standard.description: use interaction skills for identified purposes and situations, including when supporting or challenging the stated or implied meanings of spoken texts in presentations or discussion
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can use interaction skills in a range of spoken contexts, including formal and informal discussion, and use active listening to evaluate spoken texts (AC9E7LY02). They have not yet focused specifically on using interaction skills to support or challenge the stated or implied meanings of spoken texts — engaging with the substance of what is said, not just participating in discussion.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use interaction skills for identified purposes in a range of contexts, including when supporting or challenging the stated or implied meanings of spoken texts.

nodes.label: Identifying stated and implied meanings in spoken texts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can listen to a conversation or speech, identify the point being made, and explain both the tone and manner of presentation — distinguishing stated from implied meanings.
nodes.minimum_width: Listen to a spoken text, identify the explicit point being made and one implied meaning, and explain how the tone or manner of presentation signals the implied meaning.
nodes.typical_width: Listen to a range of spoken texts; identify stated and implied meanings; explain the tone and manner of presentation; describe how the interaction between explicit and implicit meaning shapes the overall message.
wider: Analyse how a formal speech uses understatement, irony or indirect language to imply positions without stating them directly — examining what the speaker does not say as well as what they say
Compare how stated and implied meanings operate differently in informal conversation vs formal debate, examining how context affects the balance between explicit and implicit communication
Investigate how First Nations or multicultural communication styles may use indirect expression, silence or implied meaning differently from mainstream Australian English interaction conventions

response_modes.reason: The distinction between stated and implied meaning in spoken language is more challenging than in written text — the cues are prosodic and contextual rather than linguistic alone. Explicit scaffolding of what to listen for — tone, pace, word choice, what's conspicuously absent — is needed before students can do this independently.

success_criteria: Identifies the explicit point being made in a spoken text.
Identifies at least one implied meaning and explains the cues (tone, manner, word choice) that signal it.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to use interaction strategies to support or challenge the implied meanings of spoken texts. Students who cannot distinguish stated from implied meaning in the first place can only engage with surface content in discussion — the interaction strategies at Node 2 have no target to work on.

nodes.label: Supporting and challenging meaning in discussion
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use effective interaction strategies — speaking clearly, asking questions about stated and implied ideas, restating and summarising — to support or challenge the meanings of spoken texts in presentations and discussion.
nodes.minimum_width: In a discussion, use at least one strategy (asking a question, restating an idea, summarising) to either support or challenge a meaning expressed by another speaker.
nodes.typical_width: Use a range of interaction strategies — speaking clearly at appropriate length, asking probing questions about stated and implied ideas, restating and summarising — to engage constructively in formal and informal discussion, including when supporting or challenging claims.
wider: Participate in a structured debate or Socratic discussion where the explicit goal is to challenge implied as well as stated meanings, using evidence-based questioning strategies
Practise summarising an opposing speaker's argument accurately and fairly before challenging it — developing the discipline of steelmanning before critique
Reflect on own interaction patterns in discussion — what assumptions do you bring? When do you challenge and when do you defer? — and evaluate how your patterns affect the quality of discussion

response_modes.reason: Effective interaction strategies need to become habitual and varied — students need a repertoire of moves (question types, summary formulations, challenge framings) rather than a single default move. Multiple discussion contexts across different formalities build this repertoire.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Structured academic controversy, Socratic discussion and formal debate formats offer rich contexts for developing sophisticated interaction skills that go well beyond minimum participation. For advancing students, meta-reflection on their own interaction patterns is particularly productive.
success_criteria: Uses at least one named interaction strategy (question, restatement, summary) purposefully during a discussion.
Can explain how the strategy was used to support or challenge a stated or implied meaning.
